edits.purpose: Correct the pooling/projection and information-limit argument
edits.before: Variability confined to the stimulus-encoding dimensions cannot be averaged away by pooling more units, because it grows with the population the same way the signal does, and it therefore bounds the information the population carries \cite{zohary1994correlated, moreno2014information}. Variability in orthogonal dimensions, however, would be removed by that same pooling operation.
edits.after: A readout that projects onto stimulus-coding dimensions can reject variability orthogonal to those dimensions. Variability overlapping those dimensions cannot be removed by this projection without also discarding stimulus-related responses; its effect on information depends on the decoding task and the detailed covariance structure \cite{zohary1994correlated, moreno2014information}.

edits.purpose: Clarify what subspace overlap implies for a downstream reader
edits.before: Shared variability aligned with neuronal tuning is conventionally read as a limit on the information a population carries, because a decoder cannot distinguish it from a change in the stimulus \cite{moreno2014information, kohn2016correlations}. That reading assumes the modulating variable is internal and unavailable to the readout, which fixational eye movements are not. The alignment we measured therefore specifies what a downstream stage must either know or infer to read the population correctly, rather than bounding what the population encodes.
edits.after: The consequence of this overlap depends on what a downstream circuit reads out and whether it has access to signals that distinguish retinal displacement from changes in the external scene \cite{moreno2014information, kohn2016correlations}. Our measurements characterize this overlap without determining how downstream circuits use eye-movement information.
edits.marked_after: \reviewedit{The consequence of this overlap depends on what a downstream circuit reads out and whether it has access to signals that distinguish retinal displacement from changes in the external scene \cite{moreno2014information, kohn2016correlations}. Our measurements characterize this overlap without determining how downstream circuits use eye-movement information.}

edits.purpose: End on the demonstrated contribution and its broader relevance
edits.before: Foveal vision is therefore a continuous sensorimotor process in which sensor motion and neural computation operate together: the eye transforms the retinal input, cortical circuits transform the resulting spatiotemporal signal, and neural activity can in turn guide subsequent sampling \cite{vonholst1950reafferenzprinzip,gibson2014ecological,ahissar2016perception}.
edits.after: Our results show that accounting for retinal image motion changes how cortical variability is interpreted and reveals a visual signal that can sharpen spatial representations.
